lead: V2X (vehicle-to-everything) is radio communication between a vehicle and the things around it: other vehicles, roadside units, pedestrians' phones and the cellular network, plus, for an electric car, the power grid. It exists because radar and cameras see only in a line of sight and cannot know what another driver intends; a V2V message can say "I am braking hard" before the brake lights ahead are visible, or warn of a car about to cross a blind junction. The same connected electronics bring live traffic, emergency calls, over-the-air updates and phone projection into the cabin, which is why connected vehicles and infotainment are taught together.
prereq: You need gateways, which keep connected units away from safety buses, and the idea of latency from vehicle networking.

blocks.text: The vehicle carries an on-board unit (OBU), a radio with a small computer. A roadside unit (RSU) is a fixed radio box at a junction, toll plaza or gantry, linked to traffic signals and to a back-end server. The links are:

items: V2V, vehicle to vehicle: position, speed and braking shared directly between OBUs.
V2I, vehicle to infrastructure: OBU to RSU, for signal timing, road works and tolling.
V2P, vehicle to pedestrian: usually a phone app or a wearable tag; important where two-wheelers and walkers share the road.
V2N, vehicle to network: through the cellular network to cloud services.
V2G, vehicle to grid: an electric vehicle that charges, or sends power back, under control messages from the grid operator. Here the main flow is power; the messages only manage it.

blocks.text: V2V, V2I and V2P can work directly, with no SIM or tower; only V2N needs cellular coverage. A safety message carries position, speed, heading, brake status and a time stamp, about ten times a second. From these the receiving OBU predicts paths and warns of: forward collision (the car ahead brakes hard), intersection movement (a car about to cross your path at a blind junction), an approaching emergency vehicle, a road hazard (crash, pothole, oil), and GLOSA (green light optimal speed advisory), which suggests a speed that reaches the next signal on green. GLOSA advises the driver; it does not change the signal.

blocks.where: d is the distance (m) at which a warning must reach the driver; v<sub>r</sub> is the closing speed (m/s); t<sub>w</sub> is the warning time the driver needs (s); Δt is the radio and processing latency (s).

sections.h3: Radio choices, the telematics unit and cloud services

blocks.text: Two radio families compete. IEEE 802.11p (DSRC in the USA, ITS-G5 in Europe) is Wi-Fi adapted for cars in the 5.9 GHz band; it works ad hoc, with no base station or subscription, and is mature. C-V2X (cellular V2X, first LTE-V2X and now 5G NR-V2X) has a sidelink, a direct device-to-device mode (PC5) that works without a tower, plus the normal network link for V2N. Both send small, frequent, signed messages; they differ in radio design and in who builds the roadside network.

The telematics control unit (TCU) is the car's cellular gateway: a modem, a GNSS receiver for position and time, and an embedded SIM. It carries live traffic, remote diagnostics, emergency call after a crash, stolen-vehicle tracking and over-the-air (OTA) updates, where the maker sends new software over the cellular link. The TCU reaches the in-car buses only through the gateway, which keeps cloud traffic away from the powertrain and chassis domains. Some cars combine the V2X OBU and the TCU in one box.

The head unit is the cabin computer behind the central screen. It plays audio and video, runs navigation (GNSS plus map data, with live traffic from the TCU), handles hands-free calls over Bluetooth, and projects a phone with Android Auto or Apple CarPlay: the phone runs the apps, and the head unit gives the screen, touch and speakers. A head-up display (HUD) can show speed, a turn arrow or a V2X warning on the windscreen; its optics belong with the instrument cluster and head-up displays. Media travels from the head unit to amplifier and displays over MOST or Ethernet.

Connection widens the attack surface: the cellular link, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, the OTA server and the diagnostic socket. A false message could fake a brake warning or unlock a door. V2X messages are therefore signed: each carries a digital signature and a certificate from a public-key infrastructure (PKI), so a receiver can check that a real OBU sent it and that it was not altered. A signature proves origin and integrity; it does not hide the content. Short-lived pseudonym certificates protect drivers' privacy, and certificates of misbehaving units can be revoked.

A connected autonomous vehicle uses V2X as one more sensor beside radar (range and speed), camera (lanes, signs) and lidar (a 3-D point cloud). V2X adds what is out of sight and what others intend. The fusion software must weigh a late or false message against its own sensors, never trust it blindly.

examples.question: Two cars approach a blind junction with a closing speed of 40 m/s. The driver needs a warning 2.5 s before the possible collision, and the V2X link plus processing adds 100 ms. At what distance must the warning be sent, and how much of that distance is due to latency?
steps: Warning distance without latency: v<sub>r</sub> × t<sub>w</sub> = 40 m/s × 2.5 s = 100 m.
Latency in seconds: Δt = 100 ms = 0.100 s.
Extra distance closed during the latency: 40 m/s × 0.100 s = 4 m.
examples.answer: The warning must be sent when the cars are 104 m apart; 4 m of that is caused by the 100 ms latency.

examples.question: An RSU at a signal tells an approaching car that the light, 250 m ahead, turns green in 20 s and stays green for 15 s. The speed limit is 50 km/h. What speed range should GLOSA advise so that the car arrives on green without stopping?
steps: The car must arrive no earlier than 20 s and no later than 20 + 15 = 35 s from now.
Highest useful speed: 250 m ÷ 20 s = 12.5 m/s = 12.5 × 3.6 = 45 km/h (faster would arrive on red).
Lowest speed: 250 m ÷ 35 s = 7.14 m/s = 7.14 × 3.6 = 25.7 km/h (slower would miss the green).
Both are below the 50 km/h limit, so the whole range is allowed.
examples.answer: GLOSA should advise about 26 to 45 km/h; any steady speed in that range reaches the signal while it is green.

traps: V2X is radio communication, not a sensor that measures anything itself; a V2X car still needs radar and cameras, and V2X adds what they cannot see.
V2V, V2I and V2P do not need cellular coverage; only V2N and cloud services stop when there is no tower.
802.11p and C-V2X are different radios: 802.11p is ad hoc Wi-Fi at 5.9 GHz; C-V2X has a direct sidelink and a network mode.
A signature is not encryption: it proves who sent the message and that it was not changed, but anyone can still read it.
Convert milliseconds to seconds before multiplying by m/s: 100 ms is 0.1 s, so the latency adds 4 m, not 4000 m.

quiz.q: Expand OBU, RSU and TCU and say what each is.
quiz.a: On-board unit: the V2X radio and computer in the car. Roadside unit: a fixed V2X radio beside the road. Telematics control unit: the car's cellular modem, GNSS and SIM, its link to the cloud.

quiz.q: Why can V2V work with no cellular coverage?
quiz.a: The two OBUs talk directly over 802.11p or the C-V2X sidelink, with no base station or SIM; coverage matters only for V2N cloud services.

quiz.q: Closing speed 25 m/s, warning time 2.0 s, latency 80 ms. Find the warning distance.
quiz.a: d = 25 × (2.0 + 0.08) = 25 × 2.08 = 52 m, of which 25 × 0.08 = 2 m is due to latency.

quiz.q: A signal 300 m ahead turns green in 15 s and stays green 20 s. Find the GLOSA speed range.
quiz.a: Arrive between 15 s and 35 s. Highest: 300 ÷ 15 = 20 m/s = 72 km/h; lowest: 300 ÷ 35 = 8.57 m/s = 30.9 km/h. Advise about 31 km/h up to the speed limit if it is below 72 km/h.

quiz.q: What does phone projection (Android Auto, CarPlay) do?
quiz.a: The phone runs navigation, music and messages; the head unit only provides the screen, touch input, microphone and speakers.

quiz.q: Give two reasons V2X needs message signatures and one limit of signing.
quiz.a: A forged emergency-braking message could cause a needless hard stop, and a spoofed position could hide a real car. Limit: a signature does not hide the content, and a real OBU with a valid certificate can still send false data, so misbehaviour detection and revocation are needed.

quiz.q: Compare 802.11p and C-V2X for an Indian city junction.
quiz.a: 802.11p is mature and needs no network, but someone must install RSUs at every junction. C-V2X can use existing towers for V2N and has a direct sidelink for V2V and V2P, so it suits areas with good coverage. For safety both use direct links; the choice is about cost, spectrum and who runs the roadside network.

beyond: Not for the exam. 5G NR-V2X adds very low latency for cooperative driving, and roadside units are gaining edge computers that fuse camera data and broadcast it as cooperative perception. Search for C-V2X PC5, cooperative awareness message, SAE J2735 and V2X PKI.
